topic: How Do James Webb Space Telescope Mirrors Stay Gold in Space?
angle: A multi-billion dollar space telescope uses a coating of pure gold that is 1,000 times thinner than a human hair to survive the harsh vacuum of space.
why: Space exploration and hardware explainers consistently draw massive viral engagement (e.g., Veritasium and Zack D. Films style shorts surpass tens of millions of views). This topic is irresistible because using actual precious gold on the most advanced telescope in history sounds like a billionaire gimmick, but is actually an essential piece of space engineering physics.
facts: The James Webb Space Telescope relies on 18 hexagonal primary mirror segments to capture light from the early universe.
Each mirror segment is made of beryllium, a metal chosen because it is extremely strong, lightweight, and holds its shape at extreme sub-zero temperatures.
Beryllium alone does not reflect infrared light efficiently, so the mirrors are coated with a microscopically thin layer of pure gold.
The gold coating is only 100 nanometers thick, which is roughly 1,000 times thinner than a single human hair.
Despite being so thin, the gold layer used on all 18 segments weighs a mere 48.2 grams (about 1.7 ounces) in total.
Gold is selected because it is the ultimate reflector of infrared light, reflecting roughly 98 percent of the infrared photons that hit it.
Because gold is a soft metal and prone to damage, a microscopic layer of silicon dioxide (glass) and amorphous carbon is applied right over it to protect it from space dust and debris.
The mirrors operate at a bone-chilling minus 388 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 233 degrees Celsius) while shielded by a tennis-court-sized sunshield.
If the mirrors were made of standard glass like the Hubble Space Telescope, they would warp and crack under the intense thermal shifts of deep space.
The gold is vaporized in a vacuum chamber and applied atom by atom onto the polished beryllium substrates.
Without this specific gold coating, the telescope would be blind to the oldest, most distant galaxies in the universe because older light shifts into the infrared spectrum.
The total cost of the gold used on the mirrors is valued at hundreds of thousands of dollars, making it a tiny fraction of the telescope's 10-billion-dollar price tag.
